utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Stojanovic. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I would just like to present Mr. Christopher Gosnell [phoen], our legal consultant in the Defence of Mr. Borovcanin. He's here for the first time in this courtroom, so I'm just using this opportunity to present him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Welcome. Mr. Stojanovic is not here; otherwise, I think we are a full house. On the Prosecution, it's Mr. Thayer and Mr. Nicholls. Is there anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart, as always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But she is happy with not being mentioned. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. Mr. McCloskey apologises for his absence this morning. We spoke with him yesterday. He is immobilized with a recurring back injury that kicked in Saturday, so he has been flat on his back and unable to do anything, other than pick up the phone. I spoke with him this morning. He is still flat on his back, so he will not be joining us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We are prepared to proceed with all of our submissions. I will take up Mr. McCloskey's anticipated submission with respect to Mr. Borovcanin. I think we're fairly confident that we will be able to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please send him a message from the Trial Chamber, wishing him a quick recovery, and not to get the impression in his mind for even a minute that this is a knock-out by the Defence teams. So let's start. If you finish today, I think that would be better because it gives us more time, and also we can come back with our decision a couple of days earlier than we had anticipated. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and may it please the Court. I will address the Court now regarding the accused Gvero and Miletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Together or one after the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: One after the other, but to some degree it will necessarily be overlapping, as I will shortly describe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm going to discuss, for a few minutes, some of the evidence about how the VRS Main Staff operated, and then the evidence, how the Main Staff directives flowed through the subordinate commands. What I hope, Your Honours, is that this will be helpful both in responding to certain issues which were raised on Friday, particularly by the Miletic Defence in its submissions, and also when I turn to review just some of the evidence necessary for 98 bis purposes which shows the two accuseds' contributions toward the forcible transfer, JCE, and to showing the forseeability of the opportunistic killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt at an early stage, but perhaps I should make this objection now. We do not understand why my learned friend needs to address my client's role at all. The submissions that we made were purely legal ones relating to deportation. There was a small subsidiary submission in relation to opportunistic killings. Neither of those submissions touched at all on General Gvero's role in this indictment. We made no mention whatsoever about that. We do not purport to make any submissions so far as that is concerned; and if it would help, a concession in relation to all counts, bar the opportunistic one and count 8, then we're quite prepared to make that concession. We never made any submission, and we fail to understand why the Prosecution are entitled to respond, let alone need to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. One moment. Do you wish to comment or reply to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Mr. President. I'm very much aware that the Gvero team did not submit on count 7, and my presentation, such as it is with respect to the evidence concerning count 7, is limited and, again, was designed to provide the underpinning for my discussion of the foreseeability of the opportunistic killings. I could dispense, should the Court deem it appropriate, with the vast, vast majority of my submission with respect to count 7, as it pertains to the accused Gvero. I'll take guidance from the Trial Chamber on that. I'm certainly prepared to keep this as short as necessary for the purposes for which we are here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I could help further on the foreseeability of the opportunistic killings. That was not the submission. The submission was purely the actus reus of the offences set out in paragraph 31, nothing to do with my client's state of mind whatsoever. Conceded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have no doubt in our mind, the four of us, that Mr. Josse is right, so please limit your submissions to address the points raised by Mr. Josse in his intervention, and the same applies -- I don't know what you were going to say in relation to Miletic, but we come to that if and when.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I was certainly happy -- I'm happy to do that, Your Honour. I was prepared to limit my remarks with respect to General Gvero and count 7. So I'll proceed. With respect to the Miletic submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Something occurs to my mind, that when Mr. Josse started his submissions last week, he said that he was not going to deal with count 7; however, in relation to count 7, he did refer to the submission made by Mr. Bourgon earlier on and expressed his opinion, and suggested that the legal issue raised by Mr. Bourgon should not be decided at the Rule 98 bis stage. I don't know, with that, if you or Mr. Nicholls meant to address that when dealing with the Nikolic case; however, that's the only thing that Mr. Josse raised in relation to count 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In responding to the submissions of the Miletic team from last Friday, I think it would be helpful to spend just a few minutes, again, talking about the evidence of the operation of the Main Staff. The presentation from the Miletic Defence team was quite far-reaching and all-embracing in some respects. It was quite factually based. I certainly don't intend to respond point by point; but in order to provide the basis for responding to some of these issues, I'd just like to go into some of the evidence concerning the Main Staff, in general, and the directives. There was evidence adduced on the record that the VRS was a disciplined army, where the chain of command and rank were respected and where orders were followed. There was a clear reporting chain which linked the Main Staff to its subordinate commands, and there was also evidence that these subordinate commands were expected to report back up that chain. In fact, there was testimony that they were duty-bound to do so. With respect to the higher-level officers, there was evidence that the former JNA officers who comprised the VRS officer corps filled those positions from the top down and that those officers were well trained and highly educated. There was evidence that starting from the Main Staff, through the subordinate commands, there were regular inspections of the subordinate commands, and that deficiencies were corrected as a result of those inspections. There is evidence on this record, Your Honours, that the VRS consistently sent its representatives forward in connection with its military operations; for example, let me turn to just one particular document, the 1993 Main Staff combat readiness analysis. That's Exhibit 414, where it observed that the "presence of the commander of the Main Staff or representative of the Main Staff, in the units carrying out the mission of the liberation of Podrinje, is a specific way of giving weight to and steering combat operations towards a single goal." Now, on the 1st of May, 1993, we see a Main Staff combat order for the liberation of Zepa and Gorazde, and the Main Staff, we see there, established an IKM at Rogatica from which it was to coordinate this operation; and, again, this touches on some themes that were brought up in the submissions. In this case, indeed, General Miletic was to be responsible, from that Rogatica IKM, for merging, planning, linking, and command and control of the forces engaged in the liberation of Zepa. Now, you heard General Smith's observations about the VRS practice of placing assistant commanders forward with the subordinate command, and this is also discussed in his expert statement. I want to briefly just discuss, read to you a quote from General Tolimir's address to the RS National Assembly on 6 August 1995, and I think this really encapsulates and will give you the flavour of how this Main Staff and its officers operated. He said, and this is at the transcript 17810 to 17811, and this is Exhibit 2953: "We are the smallest General Staff in the world among all General Staffs, either in peace or war; and all the officers of the General Staff are at the front. General Miletic is currently in the General Staff, and it was always so. General Milosevic will not be left alone, as he never was in the past. We were always sending someone from the General Staff, and we are still doing it. "There is a forward command post that is stronger than his command is, and it is located in that part of the Sarajevo front. There are two forward command posts of the General Staff in his zone. We have been keeping General Milovanovic as the most experienced commanding officer, as well as General Mladic at Granovo-Glamoc front, and in line with the part of the Main Staff and the operations for four to five months. "We make expert analyses, we prepare directives, and based on those directives we all go to the field and work in accordance with the assignments we receive." Your Honours, there is also evidence in this record that the Main Staff officers, as general officers, carried out their commander's intent via his derived authority. We heard this from Generals Milovanovic, Smith, PW-168, and, finally, Mr. Butler. And these generals, the evidence has shown, were equipped to handle their responsibilities qua generals. Here's how General Milovanovic described it: "Every general, by virtue of the fact that he was promoted into general, loses his branch designation. By virtue of being promoted into general, every general is practically promoted into a general military commander. He can command any type of unit, infantry, artillery, and so on." And he goes on to say that, by virtue of being a general, they had the skills and knowledge to conduct military operations; that is, to lead troops into combat. Now, what did General Smith have to say about his observations on the ground? This is what he said concerning his observations of Generals Gvero and Tolimir: "They could cover the full range of the responsibilities for the matter for which he was put forward to handle. The title covers the general area of a specific staff function and ensured that when the Main Staff were all together and forward headquarters aren't out there... --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- ... you've got someone focusing on making sure that's going on in the direction everyone wants it to go. "But if you've put one of these forward headquarters forward, and if you put one of these senior commanders in it, then he's commanding in your name," in this case, in General Mladic's name, "across the whole range of responsibilities."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse. I suppose you're going to reply to what you said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. With respect, he seems to be going against the ruling, and, Your Honour, the point is this: I chose not to make a speech like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right, Mr. Josse. I don't think you need to. Please, I think we made ourselves clear. Ms. Fauveau did deal with count 7, but not Mr. Josse. So I know this may have been prepared beforehand and you had General Gvero and General Miletic put together in the same basket, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have already excised much of my Gvero references but this is relevant to what happens, and I'll get into this, when somebody like PW-168 calls the Main Staff and asks for any general. And that is why I'm continuing with that type of a recitation to the Court, so that we get that larger context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But each time you mention General Gvero, you are prompting Mr. Josse to stand up, and asked to agree with him, come back to you, and we've lost five minutes in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I see the "G" word, Mr. President, I'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In this practice, we saw echoed with General Nikolai, who observed that when he was dealing with the VRS, the only useful answers he got was from the generals because they were the only ones who appeared to him to be authorised to make decisions. And if we may just go into private session very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn now to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn now to a general discussion, I'll try to make it as brief as possible, about the directives; and, again, this will ultimately respond to submissions made by the Miletic team. The evidence is that directive 7 was not drafted in a vacuum. You've heard plenty about the six strategic objectives. You've heard about the description of the military situation in the Podrinje and the Drina Valley. We see how, from the very beginning, there was this shared goal of pushing the Muslim population out. We see the Drina Corps communicate this to the Zvornik Brigade in November of 1992, and this is in Exhibit 29, pursuant to directive 4: "Force the Muslim population to leave the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde." Again, picking up directly from directive 4 from November of 1992. Now, Mr. McCloskey referred on Friday to the VRS's success in the Cerska campaign and how that forced the population into Srebrenica, and I recognise that some of these are adjudicated facts that the Court has found, so I'm not going to dwell on. But, again, I refer Your Honours to the April 1993 Main Staff combat readiness analysis, which specifically stated that: "The VRS was accomplishing," at that early stage, "the Supreme Command's strategic objectives through its operations in the Podrinje." And, again, that's relevant to General Miletic because we see, on 1 May 1993, him drafting a combat order for that liberation of Zepa and Gorazde; and if you look at that combat order, you see it reflects his deep understanding of not only the military situation but the larger political and, indeed, diplomatic situation in which this planned military operation nested. By July of 1994, we see the brigades, again, picking up on this shared goal. The commander of the Bratunac Brigade sent to all members these words: "We must continue to arm, train, discipline, and prepare the RS Army for the execution of this crucial task: The expulsion of Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave. "There will be no retreat when it comes to the Srebrenica enclave. We must advance. The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible, so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 3177, Mr. President, from Commander Ognjenovic. About the same time, we see, in 2667, 24 July 1994, the Drina Corps Commander Zivanovic, pursuant to briefings with and orders from the Main Staff, ordering the Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde enclaves reduced to their urban areas, which, as the evidence has been presented to the Court, would trigger the same resulting humanitarian crisis as we saw in 1993. And, of course, this is what brings us to P5, directive 7, drafted by the accused Miletic, 8 March 1995. I won't quote the entire language, which I think by now you've heard so many times, but the lineage from directive 4 through all these various planned operations, through these orders down through the corps to the brigades, is here again: "The unbearable situation of total insecurity, with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." Then there is the portion with respect to the restrictive issuing of permits, limiting the logistical supply of UNPROFOR, and the supply of material, resources to the Muslim population. Now, while I'm at this point, I'd like to correct one statement from my learned friend from the Miletic team from last Friday, when she said that, at page 11277 of the transcript: "General Milovanovic stated that President Karadzic may have added this sentence against the will and wish of General Miletic and that, anyway, even if General Miletic had opposed this, this opposition would have led to nothing." Let's look at the actual question and answer. Question: "You, yourself, have told us that you were not present in the Main Staff when this directive was drafted. Is it true that you don't know whether General Miletic objected to the decision made by Radovan Karadzic on carrying out this task? Did he oppose Radovan Karadzic?" The answer was: "I don't know. But even if he had, it would have been in vain." But he doesn't know. He doesn't admit that that may have been the case. He just doesn't know. There is no evidence on this record, I submit, that General Miletic in any way opposed any of the directives. The evidence, particularly at this stage of the proceedings, is quite to the contrary; and we'll see just one example in his meticulous and relentless execution of the restrictive convoy policy and his active contributions to the attacks on Srebrenica and Zepa. Now, my friend from the Miletic team also argued that directive 7-1 somehow overroad or overruled directive 7 and removed that language with which we are all so familiar from directive 7. However, if you look at the Drina Corps and brigade orders, and I believe Mr. Nicholls will address one of these, which flowed from directive 7 and 7-1, you'll see that directive 7-1 was decidedly not overwritten by 7-1; that is, obviously directive 7 was not overwritten by 7-1. For example, both the Drina Corps order and the actual attack order to the brigades for Krivaja-95 specifically refer to directive 7 and 7-1 of the VRS Main Staff. As we all know, in Exhibit 107, that attack order for Krivaja-95, it states that, pursuant to directive 7 and 7-1 of the VRS Main Staff, the objective is to split apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica and to reduce them to their urban areas. Again, evidence, at this stage of the proceedings, supports that there was the knowledge that this would create this humanitarian crisis again. And I would invite Your Honours to look at the last page of that Krivaja-95 attack order, which states that it was typed in two copies and, in fact, delivered to the VRS Main Staff; and, again, that's Exhibit 107. Now, my learned friend Mr. Haynes, in his remarks of last Friday, I believe, misstated the evidence when he stated that: "They had PW-168 here, they had Miodrag Dragutinovic here, they had Mirko Trivic here; and neither of those men, those latter men active in tactical Group 1, gave evidence of their understanding of the purpose or the objective of Krivaja-95 were." That was at pages 75 and 76. Now, I asked Colonel Trivic, the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade commander, specifically, and this was at page 11810: "And, sir, what was the main objective, as you understood it, of this operation?" His answer was: "The main objective of the operation that was set out by the corps command, as a result of the events in the previous years and months in advance that preceded this decision, was to separate the protected areas of Zepa and Srebrenica." And he went on, on page 18, 11811, to state that: "These units had the task of separating the enclaves, and that implied a narrowing down of the territory in which they were active." He continued on the next page: "First came the separation, and from that follows automatically a narrowing down of the area." And prompted by an intervention by Mr. Meek about whether that meant reducing the geographic size or the population somehow, the answer was: "Sir, I presume we've been understanding each other, that we are talking about the geographical size of the enclaves, and not the ..." -- Actually, I'm sorry, that was my question: "... not the numbers of the population; is that correct?" And his answer was: "Yes, yes." So, clearly, Mr. Trivic did have -- Colonel Trivic did have a very clear idea, from his perspective, what the Krivaja-95 operation was designed to do. Now, Mr. Haynes also claimed that: "There is not one word of evidence in this case which would support a finding that Vinko Pandurevic knew one of the main objectives of the attack was to force the Muslim population to leave the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves." That's at page 75. Well, that simply ignores General Pandurevic's 16 July interim combat report, Exhibit 330, from which I will quote to you the last line: "I consider that the Krivaja-95 operation is not complete as long as a single enemy soldier or civilian remains behind the front line." I would add, incidentally, that Nedeljko Trkulja, Colonel Trkulja, testified that he believes that General Pandurevic's 16 July interim combat report was, in fact, sent to the Main Staff at that time. So, Your Honours, this is a compelling example, I would submit, of the longstanding, consistent, and shared goal of expelling the Muslim population coming full circle back to the Main Staff. It's against this contextual backdrop that I would like to turn to discussing how General Miletic contributed to this goal of forcibly removing the Muslim population from Srebrenica and Zepa. We heard a lot from General Milovanovic about General Miletic's role both as chief of operations and when he was standing in for the chief of staff, General Milovanovic. Let me just begin by saying that Milovanovic testified that General Miletic arrived in July of 1992, just a couple of months after the VRS Main Staff itself was formed; and General Milovanovic singled him out as a particularly goods operation -- particularly good operations officer. He described what he called the collegiums, the daily Main Staff meetings, which would be attended by the assistant commanders. And allow me to quote somewhat extensively from some of General Milovanovic's testimony because my learned friend really challenged the clarity of General Miletic's responsibilities and authority, and I think there is plenty of evidence, particularly at this stage, which shows what those responsibilities and authorities were. This is at the transcript pages 12188 to 12189: "Every morning at 7.00, there is a meeting of the Main Staff. Usually, it is the inner circle, which means General Mladic, with all his assistants; and regularly these morning meetings were attended by the chief of operations administration, the chief of intelligence administration, and the security administration, in addition to the assistant commanders. "And it would usually be the commander, General Mladic, who would call the meeting to order, and he would give the floor to General Miletic, standing in for the chief of staff, and then we, either me or him, would inform all the present about the problems in the theatre of war, and we would draw each sector's chief to what they had to pay attention. After the meeting, chiefs of sectors would study the details that their attention had been drawn to and that they provide proposals to the commander. Usually, it would happen immediately during the first meeting. If there was a lot of such thing, then there would be a need for us to meet either once or twice during the course of the same day. "This was a system that was in place; and based on this system, Miletic obtained this particular information. It did happen that the commander was not in staff, the chief of staff was not in the staff, and then the most senior general would chair the meeting. But Miletic, again, was the one who explained the situation, who provided an insight into the situation based on the reports." General Milovanovic went on further to describe how critical General Miletic's contribution was to this nerve centre. He said, at page 12305 to 12309: "Miletic's trench was to design documents, to make plans, to coordinate the work of subordinated units, with a view to accomplishing the uniform task of all VRS units, and that is to defend Republika Srpska. Miletic did this as an officer of the staff. The value of every operations officer is great, is crucial, but operations officers are considered to be the soul of the army." In this case, he was the soul of the Main Staff of the VRS. He knows everyone. He is able to advise everyone to give them the appropriate information. Indeed, he was "a figure who united and coordinated the work of the Main Staff and was always present." Now, again, my learned friend said that there was confusion, that nobody really knows what "standing in for the chief of staff" really means and what exactly are the functions and duties. And, again, I think General Milovanovic made that pretty clear, and this is at 12305 of the transcript: "When he substituted for me, he had to coordinate the work of assistant commanders, but not in an order-issuing sense, but rather in an advisory role. I don't know which word to use. Perhaps the best word is a non-binding sense. "As deputy chief of staff, it was his duty to tell a general that he has a problem in his sector. So he was the one that coordinated, but not in the sense of issuing orders. That was something that General Mladic could do, or I in Mladic's absence. "But he could tell Gvero, 'Go to that logistical unit and check why there are so many violations and infractions. It's beginning to affect morale.' He could tell Djukic, 'Find those units and materiel.' So he could not really speak in a commanding tone. "He could tell others, 'This sector needs such-and-such supplies and assistance.'" And in response to a question from His Honour Judge Agius, General Milutinovic stated that General Miletic would "certainly do it without consulting me, because in order to consult me he would have had to establish contact with me across 600 or 700 kilometres, and there would be no need for the enemy to be allowed to listen in." In response to another question, he continued: "If General Mladic was at the Main Staff, then my role would be the same as the role I have described for Miletic a moment ago. I was also an assistant commander, except that I was the first among equals, in a way. However, if Mladic was not around, then I did have a command role. I could order Miletic or Djukic to give Gvero what he needed. Miletic was never in a position to issue orders to assistant commanders." Now, again, in response to a question by His Honour, in the event that neither Generals Mladic or General Milovanovic would be present, who would be in a position to issue orders, he answered: "No one. In that case, General Miletic would have had to call him, regardless of distance; but if the case in question called for it, if it was an emergency, he could have called General Milovanovic, or if General Mladic were closer, he would have had to call General Mladic, so that one of them could issue appropriate orders." General Milovanovic continued: "However, in practice, in the practice of the Main Staff, such situation never arose because, after all, the Main Staff was a harmonious whole. We had a good mutual understanding, and I can't imagine a situation in which General Gvero would refuse the advice of General Miletic, and I can't imagine any of the assistant commanders having any quarrel with what Miletic proposed. We just never experienced such incidents." He said it a number of times, and he finally said it again at 12309: "I have already said a number of times that General Miletic substituted for me in performing day-to-day staff duties during my absences from the staff." So it's no surprise that Colonel Sladojevic testified that when he reported to the Main Staff on the morning of 13 July: "I was received by General Miletic. He told me that he was the chief of the operations and education administration..." --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- "... and that he was also performing the duties of the chief of staff in the chief of staff's absence." That's at 14359 of the transcript. With respect to General Miletic's role as an adviser, General Milovanovic stated that General Miletic was certainly not General Mladic's main man, but whether he ever provided any advice to General Mladic: "Well, he probably did. Sometimes when my functions were distributed to others in my absence, then Miletic would suggest to Mladic how to use units, and advising the commander amounts to giving the commander your opinion how that should be done. And Miletic could do that because he was the best informed on the situation in various theaters of war in Republika Srpska when I was not there." And, again, that's at 12311 of the transcript. General Miletic, according to General Milovanovic, had influence in the sense that when General Milovanovic was in Western Bosnia: "When I asked for three brigades, he answered that the Main Staff could not send me those brigades, and he explained why. "Also, if I approached the Main Staff in order to request additional materiel, ammunition, fuel, and so forth, he would convey my messages to the commander of the Main Staff or the assistant commander for logistics; or if I had problems with the state of morale, he would convey those as well. "In other words, he was my intermediary in my communication with the other members of the Main Staff and very often even with the Supreme Command." That's at 12317 to 12318. And, finally, General Milovanovic testified at 12319 again: "Of course, General Miletic could participate in discussions because he was standing in for me, and he could convey proposals to the commander, just like me, because he was familiar with the corps reports. He was familiar with the situation, based on my conversations with him; and he could explain the situation in Western Bosnia as well as I could have myself." Now, I want to spend just a few minutes discussing the evidence concerning General Miletic's role in enforcing the VRS restrictions on convoys, and I won't subject everyone to secondary convoy terror by throwing out individual convoy reports ad nauseam. But my friend asked: Do we have evidence that the restrictions -- or the restriction to humanitarian aid increased after the directive. The answer is: Absolutely. PW-106, and I'll just cite, I won't read from all these selections, but I'll just draw the Court's attention to the testimony of PW-106 on November 15th of 2006 at page 3938; the testimony of Major Ruten November 29th, 2006, page 4797; the testimony of PW-155, 5 February 2007, pages 6829, and that's at line 17 through 23, and page 6830, beginning at line 3; the testimony of Meho Dzebo the 28th of March, 2007, page 9595. With respect to the restrictions and the effect of those restrictions on the operational state of effectiveness for the Dutch-Bat Battalion, I barely need to mention the names of Franken, Koster, Van Duijn, Runin, and others, to remind the Chamber that there is ample evidence that the restrictions on the Dutch-Bat re-supply tightened even further after directive 7 was issued. Specifically, there was the testimony about the fuel convoys. Not limited to that, but that's something that certainly stood out in witnesses' minds with particular clarity as to the date. General Milovanovic testified that even after the cooperation committee was formed, the VRS continued to control the convoys, and that was at 12290 of the transcript. You heard that there was Colonel Djurjic, a member of the Main Staff, on that commission. Let me just recite some exhibit numbers. Again, I want to spare you putting them up again: 2651A invites you to look at the detail of General Miletic's restrictions there; 2714, 2 June 1995, denying school supplies, fuel for saws; 2717, restricting rotation of an NGO; 2497, the 18 June 1995 document, General Miletic demanding a detailed check; 2551, 29 June, referring to the UNMO rotation and working with Momir Nikolic; 2570, General Miletic telling the Bratunac Brigade that the brigade security organs must monitor the Medevac. We've seen the exhibits, the documents showing that the brigades implemented these restrictions. I invite you to recall Colonel Trivic's testimony about what would happen if the brigade didn't carry out General Miletic's instruction; for example, on 27 -- I'm sorry, 2497, demanding the accounting of the items. He said it's inconceivable that they wouldn't comply, and he presumes that they reported back to the Main Staff. That's at 12043. And, again, my learned friend made a big point of arguing that General Miletic was not in the field, was not on the ground during the attacks on Srebrenica and Zepa. Of course, he wasn't. That's because, as we've seen, General Smith -- I'm sorry, long weekend -- General Miletic is performing the critical job of running the Main Staff during this period of time, holding the fort down while his chief of staff is forward. You bet he's at the Main Staff. I want to turn to some of the evidence capable of sustaining a conviction under counts 7 and 8 and focus on General Miletic's activities and his contributions during the attack on Srebrenica and Zepa. We have Exhibits 2889 and 2890, the 2nd and 3rd July Main Staff daily combat reports, and I'll talk about those in a little while, where he reports to President Karadzic that the Drina Corps is preparing for combat. And, again, recall this is the date of General Zivanovic's attack order, Krivaja-95. Again, we have this evidence that it was, in fact, sent to the VRS Main Staff on the last page. By the 6th of July, in Exhibit 2895, in the Main Staff daily combat report of that date, General Miletic mentions the combat operations towards Srebrenica and Zepa. Then we start seeing a lot of activity surrounding these events intersecting at the Main Staff, some of which General Miletic has direct participation in, some of which a reasonable inference, based on the evidence presented to Court, establishes that he would have known about. For example, we have Exhibits 2899 and 13. We have the 12 July request from General Skrbic to the Ministry of Defence for buses and the follow-up documents from the Ministry of Defence out to get those buses for the transportations at Potocari. We have Exhibit 156, 12 July Drina Corps request to the Main Staff, requesting additional fuel. This is for moving out the population pursuant to the Main Staff's order. We have Exhibit 1111, an intercept of 12 July at 1220 hours, again involving discussion of fuel and General Miletic's involvement in that. Exhibit 1112, a 1240 hours intercept of 12 July. Panorama, the code name for the Main Staff, is told about the transportations. Then we have two follow-up intercepts, one of which my learned friend talked about, 1113, at 1250 hours on 12 July, where General Mladic says: "We'll evacuate them all, those who want to and those who don't want to." Now, my friend said that doesn't involve the Main Staff, but I think the evidence supports, clearly, when we see how this Main Staff operated, that that just cannot be the case. Also, that date we have 2748, a Main Staff daily combat report, where General Miletic is reporting on women and children hitting a minefield trying to withdraw from the enclave. He specifically notes that Krivaja-95 is proceeding according to plan. He refers to the transportations, Zepa, and MUP laying ambushes. This is at 19848 to 19850 of the transcript. We'll see on the 13th, as well, a similar daily combat report from the Main Staff to President Karadzic, again mentioning the transferring of the population. On the 14th of July, we have a 2102 hours intercept where Jokic is telling Colonel Beara to call 1155. He says they're having huge problems with the people, "I mean the parcel," Jokic's words, and that the higher house urgently needs Colonel Beara. I invite Your Honours to look at Exhibit 1146, a 14 July intercept at 2227, and this is the one where one of the participants is identified as Vilotic. There is evidence in the case that this is, in fact, General Miletic, and he is speaking with Jokic. I would just invite the Chamber to look at the tone, the language that's used by Miletic in this intercept: "Don't talk to me about that. Do as I order you." Is it the Prosecution's case with respect to this, as one example, but we have others, that General Miletic is originating orders, that he's issuing orders? No, that's never been our case. The evidence from which a reasonable tribunal of fact could find is that General Miletic was passing on orders consistent with the intentions of his commander, under the derived authority of that commander, General Mladic. We have another example. This is Exhibit 2754. I think it's also been doubly numbered as 2518. This is a 15 July document in which General Miletic is moving troops; and I submit, again, that the language here is, to use Rick Butler's terminology, directional. There are a lot of "shall"s. General Milovanovic said this is the kind of work that General Milovanovic -- that he would have expected General Miletic to be doing standing in for him, warning General Pandurevic, then Colonel Pandurevic, to expect men. Again, he's not, in the Prosecution's submission, originating his orders; he's passing them on under the derived authority of General Mladic. Now, regarding the Zepa operation, we have Exhibit 183, a document dated 15 July, from General Tolimir to General Miletic, wanting to ensure that they've got secure communications in place for the Zepa operation. Then we see, again in the Main Staff daily combat report of that day, General Miletic updating President Karadzic on Zepa. If we look at 377, the duty operations officer --

In there, he says he told General Miletic that they're out of fuel. Now, this brings us to, again, the 17th of July. You'll recall that Colonel Trkulja testified that, on that date, General Miletic ordered him and Colonel Sladojevic to travel to the Zvornik Brigade, in his words, "to raise readiness on the front line." I think we're all familiar with the testimony about the nature and substance of that trip. The order from which General Miletic derived his authority is Exhibit 37, and if we could go into private session just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, with respect to the Zepa operation, Exhibit 1231 is a 17 July intercept from General Mladic to General Krstic. General Mladic says in this intercept: "Get in touch with Miletic on the secure line. Full steam ahead. I didn't accept the Turk's conditions." There is evidence in this case that this is referring to the Zepa operation. That's at 19936 of the record. We have Exhibit 2517, the notorious 21 July Tolimir chemical weapons document, and I won't go into that any further. I think you're all familiar with that. With respect to the events on the ground in Zepa, we have Exhibit 191, a 25 July communication from General Tolimir to Generals Gvero or Miletic, stating that they have a copy of the Zepa agreement, and discussing further General Tolimir's view of the situation. That night, we see, in Exhibit 190, the same date, General Miletic continuing his active role. That's at 19941 of the transcript. I'll address the Court probably after the break about the issue of the status of the men from Zepa who crossed the Drina River. That's at 12187 of the record. Mr. President, if I may --
