utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to address now the issue concerning count 8 that was raised on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In relation to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: To two issues. The first is with respect to the status of the men from Zepa who crossed the Drina River to Serbia. Let me just say, preliminarily, that we're all aware of the overall issue being currently on appeal, and our position clearly adopts the Prosecution's appellate brief in Mrksic and in Martic. So I don't have too much more to say in terms of performing any exegesis on the judgement. But let me speak for a few minutes about this issue of whether all of these men who crossed are soldiers. Some, without a doubt, among the men who crossed the river were soldiers who had been active participants in the hostilities and who had abandoned their positions and weapons to flee. Also among the men were men of military age, like PW-155, who the evidence shows were not participants in the hostilities. I'll have more to say about PW-155 in a bit. Now, my friends, understandably, focused on the VRS's perception of the swimmers, and I'll refer to them as swimmers as a shorthand, as all combatants; and we can, indeed, see, from some of the documents themselves from the VRS, that that's the premise that underlies the argument that the VRS considered any able-bodied men, male, to be a combatant. If you look at Exhibit 188, that's a Tolimir report regarding the situation in Zepa, dated 13 July 1995. Just to bring you back a little bit, Your Honours, this is where Witness 49 testified that he meets with General Tolimir on that date. General Tolimir tells him, "Srebrenica has fallen, and now it's your turn," and he puts forward two options: The complete evacuation of the entire population or a military solution. And that's at 9724. Corresponding to that meeting, we note in the report that Tolimir states: "We have also required that all able-bodied men are registered and exchange for our war prisoners in the Muslim prisons." Now, just because the VRS considered any able-bodied Muslim male to be a combatant doesn't make it so, and I'm aware of no case law to support that thesis, especially when we take a look at the evidence which obviously must be viewed in the most favourable light to the Prosecution. Let me start with General Smith. My friends cited to some of his testimony, but they, in my respectful submission, ignored his most relevant testimony on this issue. This is at page 17451, 6 November 2007. General Smith put it very concisely. With respect to Zepa, what he saw going on there, based on his observations and discussions, being briefed, there is a group of people who are fighters, who are more or less armed; and then in the pocket, in the enclave as well, there are the families and so forth, and there are men of military age who may or may not be fighters, and it was always going to be a problem of differentiating those people. "That I'd always understood, and wasn't going to be a problem you could easily solve." That was after I put a question to him in which I had asked: "Just to be specific, we're talking about not only any men who may have been in the center of Zepa, but the men of military age who were in the hills and still fighting?" It was my reference, I submit, to "still fighting" that prompted General Smith to correct me as to what he saw what was the situation on the ground at that time. And, indeed, Your Honours, after correcting me, General Smith specifically challenged my learned friend Madame Fauveau during cross-examination when she asked, at page 17634: Question: "Speaking about Zepa, men of military age, members of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zepa, they never surrendered to the Serbs, did they?" General Smith's answer was: "Are you saying that all men of military age were members of the armed forces?" And my friend answered: "Not yet. But before answering my question, maybe you could tell me what your opinion was on that particular issue." General Smith replies: "Well, I'm very happy to answer your question, but I wanted to understand the question I was being asked, and you were putting two things together which I wasn't convinced is so." There are a series of questions and answers concerning the conscription policies in the VRS and within the armija. Then at 17636, General Smith says: "If I can make only one other point: It isn't so much the manpower, it's their weapons in these circumstances; and while, of course, all those men had the potential to be a soldier, they didn't necessarily have the capacity to be one." This reality is certainly reflected in the testimony of Witness 49, whose testimony I say, with respect to my learn friend for the Gvero team, characterized rather selectively, in my opinion. My friend quoted from page 9818, so let me go directly and read it instead of characterizing. The question that was put to Witness 49 was: "That is a fair assessment, is it not, from UNPROFOR, that the 1.500 people who remained were, in fact, BiH troops?" The answer was: "That is quite a correct assessment, but these were men of the age group from 18 and maybe even under that, from 18 to 55 years of age. To what extent they were involved and engaged during the war, that's another matter, but I'm sure there weren't 1.500 who were actually armed." Witness 49 also specifically testified, and this is at 9721 of the transcript, that: "There were about 1.200 able-bodied men in Zepa, of whom only 600 to 700 were armed, and they were commanded by Colonel Polic." There is other evidence which puts the estimate of civilians left in Zepa even higher. At the transcript 18322, there is a document which refers - it's a UN document - to the UN estimating that there were 2.000 to 3.000 people left in Zepa after the transportations were completed. This document notes that the Serbs said they were all army, but the UN thought at least half were civilians. Again, not surprisingly, the VRS documents themselves reflect these differing perceptions and observations. Look at, and I invite the Court to read, P190, where it is clear that there are these categories being described by General Smith. P190 is from Lieutenant-Colonel Karanovic to General Tolimir, updating him on the events in Zepa on the 28th of July, 1995. Specifically, he's updating him with respect to the negotiations still ongoing at the Sarajevo Airport. In this document, Lieutenant-Colonel Karanovic writes that: "In order to sign this agreement, Muslims are willing to secure release of all prisoners of war demanded by the VRS. It is emphasised that it is important that civilians, disarmed soldiers, and able-bodied men are evacuated together from Zepa, and they demand guarantees that they are not going to be killed." Now I'd like to turn to PW-155. On cross-examination, on three occasions at 6873, 6876, twice on one of those pages, PW-155 specifically stated that he was not in the army. There was no evidence that he was participating in the hostilities, save for running to the lines when the VRS was about to crash the defences. There is evidence from him that once he took his family to Stitkov Dol, he never returned to the lines. I refer you to Colonel Savcic's testimony that by the 24th or the 25th of July, the 25th being when P-155 recalls bidding his family goodbye at Stitkov Dol, Colonel Savcic testified that the organised defence and resistance in Zepa had ceased. That's at 15279 of the record. Let's look at the circumstances PW-155 was in from the 25th of July through the 1st of August, when he made the decision to cross the river. He and about 50 other men were in caves, hiding up in the canyons. This is at 6837 of the transcript. My friend characterized PW-155's testimony as simply standing up to no examination at all. Well, this was a witness who became so overcome with emotion when he testified about bidding his family goodbye, the decision he had to make, that he had to take a break and leave this courtroom. He had to make another decision, to leave his brothers behind. He said that the men he was with did not know what to do. His mind was filled with thoughts of killing himself. They ultimately decided to break up into smaller groups, thinking that that would be the best way to survive. He made it across with one other person. This was no Dunkirk, this was no organised retreat, this was unarmed men fleeing for their lives. Again, using Witness 49's numbers, 500 to 600 men he believed were armed. His estimates were that 950 made it over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you do the math, that leaves a few hundred civilians, in the purest sense of the word, who made it across. Our position clearly is that P-155 was never a soldier; he was a civilian for the purposes of this period of time. Clearly, he stated that he participated in the village guards at some point. Clearly, he went to the line. But, certainly, at this stage, we have to accept his testimony, his clear and consistent testimony, that he was a civilian. And even if Your Honours find that he was a soldier, he was a combatant for that period of time, certainly when he turned his back and made for Serbia, he was hors de combat. Mr. McCloskey on Friday already referred to those men not having an option to surrender and that that was a reasonable fear. I respectfully submit to Your Honours, based on the evidence taken in the light most favourable to the Prosecution, that the evidence before the Chamber is that P-155 was a civilian; and to the extent that he had ever participated in hostilities, he had laid down whatever arms he had access to. Related to Mr. McCloskey's submission on Friday that the unlawful attack began really on 8 March of 1995, I just want to draw the Chamber's attention to the Stakic appeal judgement, which points out that force is "not limited to physical force, but includes the threat of force, or coercion, such as that caused by fear of violence, duress, detention, psychological oppression, or abuse of power against such person or persons, or by taking advantage of a coercive environment." I think the evidence has been overwhelming that that environment was coercive. That's got to be the understatement of 2008 so far. Let me just conclude by calling your attention, again, to a piece of evidence which directly speaks to that reasonable fear in those men from Zepa held, the 8 August 1995 daily combat report from Colonel Kusic referring to killing remaining "balijas" and describing specifically killing an unarmed male born in Srebrenica, 24 years old, who was looking for food. Thank you, Your Honours. I'm happy to answer any questions on these issues; otherwise, that concludes my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Nicholls, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning to my friends. I'm going to briefly respond to the arguments made on behalf of Mr. Beara and Mr. Nikolic. I'm going to take those two in reverse order and speak about Mr. Nikolic first. Some of the arguments I'll be making overlap, and so I will not address all the -- all the same topics with Mr. Beara. I'm also not going to respond to all of the arguments made on behalf of Mr. Beara and Mr. Nikolic, but just the ones I think bear a response. The first thing I want to do is point to, speaking now about the submissions made on behalf of Mr. Nikolic, a few of the errors, not necessarily all of the errors, but a few of the errors my friend made in the transcript. At 21269, Mr. Bourgon asserted that it was confirmed by Witness Richard Butler that there was no involvement by the Zvornik Brigade in the forcible transfer of women and children from Potocari and that this led to the conclusion that Drago Nikolic was also not involved. That's not the case. If you look at the pages Mr. Bourgon cited to you, 20388 to 389, Mr. Butler stated that the Zvornik Brigade was involved, at least to the extent of sending buses and trucks, and he never confirmed that Drago Nikolic was not involved. On Thursday, at 21271, my friend cited Mr. Butler, again at the same pages, to confirm, allegedly, that Drago Nikolic was not present, had the day off on 12 July. I think, if you look at what Mr. Butler said, you'll see that that is not accurate. In referring to 3DP311, the attendant's log, Mr. Butler testified that that was only an indicator that Nikolic had the day off, and he said: "The presumption is that somebody like the assistant commander for security is not going to be able to sit and enjoy his day off while the rest of the units were being told to bring all their other people in from leave. So I agree that it's an indicator that he might not be there, but I can't say that definitively." This was characterized as confirmation by Mr. Butler that Drago Nikolic was not present on the 12th. At 21273, my friend asserted: "Moreover, there is no evidence on the record on the basis of which a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that Drago Nikolic had any knowledge or was involved in any way in the capture, surrender, and detention of able-bodied men from the column." That is not correct. If you look at the very first witness in this case, PW-110, his testimony, PW-110 was a civilian who fled in the column from Potocari. He testified that he surrendered with many other men at Sandici. That's when we're only up to page 650 in this case. He described his night on the truck in Bratunac and how the next day he and the others who'd surrendered from the column were taken to the Orahovac school. He survived the execution there and identified Gojko Simic, who was shown as a member of the 4th Battalion. Drago Nikolic, the evidence has shown, overwhelming evidence has shown, was outside the school, controlling the MPs who were guarding PW-110 and the other prisoners who were inside the school. You can look to that evidence from PW-142, PW-143, PW-101, PW-168, Milorad Bircakovic and more, that Drago Nikolic was at the Orahovac school and supervised and controlled the MPs there before and during the arrival of the prisoners, and was even present, PW-101 testified, at the execution site. So is it fair, is it accurate, to say there's no evidence on the record on the basis of which a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that Drago Nikolic had any knowledge or was involved in any way in the capture, surrender, and detention of able-bodied men from the column? Similarly, at 21276, my friend stated and it was his submission that there was no evidence on the record on the basis of which a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that Drago Nikolic was involved in controlling the transportation of Muslim men from Bratunac at any time. Moreover, should the Trial Chamber conclude that Drago Nikolic was in some way involved, that this was only related to the joint criminal enterprise to kill the able-bodied men from Srebrenica. And, clearly, that participation was related, and I'll talk more about the JCEs and how they overlapped to the JCE to kill the able-bodied men from Srebrenica, but it's not accurate to say there's no evidence for a reasonable trier of fact to conclude that Drago Nikolic was not involved in controlling the transportation of the Muslim from Bratunac. If we could go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So it's clear that his task is to prepare, to receive, and to accommodate these prisoners as they come from Bratunac. Drago Nikolic's driver, Milorad Bircakovic, testified that he and Drago Nikolic met the convoy, on the 14th, of prisoners from Bratunac at the Vidikovac Hotel, and that Drago Nikolic told him to get on the first bus, which was full of prisoners, and to go to Orahovac. That's at 11054 to 11055. The convoy of prisoners then does go to Orahovac, where they are detained. There's some more evidence that I'll talk about later. Again, is it fair or accurate to say that there's no evidence on the record, when Drago Nikolic was fully engaged in preparations to receive the prisoners, to detain them, and he meets the convoy once they get to Zvornik, or to Divic, just outside? One legal point, a small -- well, it's not a small point, but I think it's an obvious point. At 21263, Mr. Bourgon stated that the mens rea for forcible transfer required the intent to permanently displace the population, and cited to a commentary to the Geneva Conventions. I just refer the Trial Chamber to the Stakic Appeals Judgement at paragraphs 307 and 317, which made clear, and it's a quote: "The mens rea does not require the intent to transfer permanently." I think we've shown that mens rea, that this forcible transfer was intended to be permanent, but it's not an element that we need to prove. I want to talk briefly now about the two JCEs in the case as they relate to forcible transfer under Article 7. The elements of forcible transfer are pretty clear and simple under Article 5. It's the forced displacement of persons by expulsion or other forms of coercion from the area in which they are lawfully present within state borders. As Mr. Thayer said, "forced" does not to be physical force or violence, it involves coercion as well. The mens rea requires simply the intent to displace a person from that place where they are lawfully present. Now, the fact that there are two JCEs in this case, forcible transfer and the murder operation, does not mean that these crimes, the forcible transfer and the murder operation, are distinct. They're completely intertwined, they're overlapping, and they're all involved with the same objective, which is to get rid of the entire Muslim population, not just the women and children, not just the men, but the population from Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. So it would be artificial and unnecessary to somehow try to separate the forcible transfer and the murder operations from each other. The indictment is also clear that the common purpose of the JCE was to force the Muslim population, as a whole, all of the Muslims, out of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. Just to make it clear, at one point, counsel for Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Beara both tried to argue that somehow the forcible transfer was over by 13 July. The forcible transfer pled, in our JCE as we've pled it, continued after 13 July, continued through to the end of August 1995. The language to areas outside the control of the RS does not define either the purpose or the goal of that crime. It is not a necessary element of the crime of forcible transfer. What the core of that crime is, that we need to prove and that we have proven at this stage, for the purposes of 98 bis, is that there was a common purpose to remove the population from the enclaves, the entire population. Now, clearly, you'd go right back to 1992, May 1992, the strategic objectives, many of the documents cited by my friend. It's clear. What was the goal? The goal was the creation of a Serb state, and the goal was to remove permanently the populations from these two enclaves, and a large part of that was to areas outside of the RS. But, again, it's not an element that needs to be proven, that they would all go outside the RS, or the area of control of the VRS. The core is that they are all removed from the enclaves unlawfully and then transported. I'd like to go through the parts of the indictment which make it clear that notice has always been, for all of the accused, that the JCE encompassed and included the transfer of all of the men out of the enclaves. Paragraph 62 specifically puts the Defence on notice that the men who were bussed from Potocari to Bratunac were victims of forcible transfer. Paragraph 63 - and I'll go over these in a bit more detail - puts the Defence on notice that the men from the column who surrendered or captured were victims of the same forcible transfer. Paragraph 48(e), under persecutions, count 6, states with absolute clarity that the men separated and those who surrendered or were captured from the column were victims of forcible transfer. All of these pieces of the whole of forcible transfer occurred within the common purpose outlined in paragraph 49. So, to sort of sum it up, there was always the JCE to cleanse, remove the population from the enclaves in their entirety. Along the way, there was a JCE to kill and murder the able-bodied men. That never negated, changed, or in any way altered the purpose that these men, all of them, be forcibly transferred out of the enclaves. It's that forcing of the men, that transfer of the men forcibly, along with the rest of the population out of the enclaves, that constitutes the criminal purpose and element of this JCE. Just one example, before I move on to the indictment. PW-118 is the Luca School survivor. He tried to survive by getting on the buses at Potocari and was taken off right before, right before he would have made it over and was separated at the border of the ABiH territory in Kladanj, and was taken to be executed and survived that execution. That man was forcibly transferred, whether or not he made it the remaining few yards into the "free territory," as they called it. If I could now go specifically to a couple of points in the indictment which both go to notice and show and illustrate my explanation. Paragraph 48(e), the forcible transfer of Bosnian Muslims from Srebrenica and Zepa by means of the forced bussing of the women and children to Bosnian Muslim controlled territory and the forced bussing of the men separated at Potocari or captured or having surrendered from the column, up to the Zvornik area, where they were ultimately executed. Count 7, forcible transfer. Just above paragraph 61, the heading: "The forceful removal of the Muslim population from Srebrenica." Paragraph 61 refers to women, children and the elderly. The next paragraph, 62, under forcible transfer, refers to the men separated at Potocari who were all removed from that area. The next paragraph, 63, the men captured or surrendered from the column. It begins: "On 13 July 1995, approximately 5.000 to 6.000 Bosnian Muslim men from the column of men escaping from the Srebrenica enclave were captured or surrendered," and it goes on. If we come now to the paragraphs outlining the role and actions of the accused in the JCE to forcibly transfer and deport, it also makes clear that all these men are included because they are part of the population. They are lawfully present in the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, and they are forcibly removed from those enclaves. Ljubisa Beara, paragraph 78 - I won't read them all out - but subparagraphs 1, 2, and 3 under 78(a) are listed as his acts and contributions to controlling the movement of the Muslim population out of the enclaves. Just as an aside, there was a lot of talk about, "Well, I wasn't in Zepa; my client wasn't in Zepa; Zepa is far away." This is a JCE. The same contributions to Srebrenica, or contributions to the JCE to remove the population from both enclaves. That's made clear - I don't have the date - on Your Honour's decision to the challenges on the indictment and the challenges to the JCE pled. Paragraph 71(a)(1), (2), and (3) describe the actions of Vujadin Popovic also related to the forcible transfer of the Muslim men from Srebrenica, including his presence in Potocari on the 12th and his actions in the transfer of the men. Sorry, Your Honours, I was referring earlier to the 72 decision of 31st May 2006. Drago Nikolic, paragraph 80, which outlines his contributions, his acts in the JCE to forcibly transfer; 80(a), controlling the movement of the population out of the enclaves; (1) and (2) show his actions; (2) specifically, the evidence I've alluded to, his actions in making sure and insisting that the men captured or separated were brought from Bratunac up to Zvornik and then to different locations, and the continuing chain of their expulsion from the enclaves. Now, of course, these paragraphs overlap with his contribution to the murder JCE. They're part of the same thing. But from these paragraphs, it's clear, and the notice is clear, that the JCE included the men separated from Potocari and those who surrendered and captured from the column, and the actions of the accused in that forcible transfer. Let me very briefly discuss Drago Nikolic's -- some of the evidence regarding his actions in the forcible transfer. The 13 July, 65 ter 647, that's the IKM log which shows that he was extraordinarily relieved from duty that night. We know, from the evidence I've just quoted in private session, why he was relieved from that duty and where he went next. We know from the evidence that late at night on the 13th, the night he's relieved from duty, he's at the Orahovac School when the first prisoners arrive. The prisoners arrive that night and then the next day. To the very best memory of PW-143, who went to the Orahovac School from the Zvornik barracks on the 13th, it is Nikolic, not Jasikovac the police commander who was there controlling the MPs that night, positioning them around the school, telling them where they should be guarding the prisoners. That's at 6532 to 6533. I asked him: "When you saw Drago Nikolic at the Orahovac School that evening, what was he doing?" Answer: "They assigned us to the places where we would be spending the night and guarding those prisoners." Question: "And, specifically, who was assigning you? You can say the name. Who was telling you where to go, where to spend the night?" Answer: "I think that was Drago Nikolic, specifically he assigned us to the places where we would be spending the night." Then he explains that includes all the military police, as well. Also, the same witness at 6612 on redirect: "Just to be very clear on this issue, to the best of your memory today, Drago Nikolic or Jasikovac, who was assigning you to the places?" "In my opinion, it was Drago Nikolic." Of course, we know from the evidence -- well, lots of evidence of the command and structure and relationship of the chief of security to military police to the security police that, whether it's Nikolic or Jasikovac, and even if Jasikovac is present, that these MPs have formally been placed at the disposal of Drago Nikolic. I'm not going to go over that evidence about the relationship of the security organs to the military police, other than to refer Your Honours to the way it was put very clearly and very well by General Milovanovic during cross-examination by my friend Mr. Bourgon. That's at 12394 to 12395, and I have a large quote. But just at the end, General Milovanovic asks: "I suppose you meant the commander, who is the chief of security superior; is that what you mean?" "Exactly, General, simply for you to confirm that although he, Drago Nikolic, may have a coordination or controlling role, he does not issue orders that come from him to the military police; he has no authority to do that?" Answer: "Correct. He does not have the authority to command the police. He can propose the commander to use the military police; and if the commander agrees to that, then he conveys the commander's orders and he gives instructions to the commander of the military police battalion or company as to what to do, how to proceed." Just a little bit above that, the General states, of the security chief: "He has the controlling role when it comes to the police." Lastly, again in regard to the actions of Drago Nikolic in the forcible transfer, look at 65 ter 905. That's the vehicle log for the car assigned to Drago Nikolic, driven by Milorad Bircakovic, which shows 13 of July, amongst others, Standard, IKM, Zvornik, Orahovac, Bratunac; 14 July, Standard, Orahovac, Divic, Orahovac, Rocevic, Orahovac, Zvornik; all the places where prisoners from Bratunac are brought to. On the 14th of July, again, according to Drago Nikolic's driver, Drago Nikolic meets the convoy of prisoners coming from Bratunac, puts Bircakovic on the front bus, and then the column of buses goes to Orahovac. Also, on the 14th of July, at 11603 to 11607, the testimony from Mr. Ostoja Stanisic that Drago Nikolic is with Beara at the crossroads near Petkovci. This is confirmed by the testimony of Marko Milosevic at 13301 to 13307. The evidence I've just described, the acts referred to in paragraph 80, demonstrate Nikolic's conduct and direct participation in the forcible transfer of the men separated from Potocari or who were surrendered and were captured from the column. He's a vital link in this chain of the movement and transfer of these men. He gets them from Bratunac and brings them to the schools, to where for most of them the transfer ends. His contribution also includes these actions and the actions in the murdering of the men, because we've seen the effect that had -- the coercive effect that had on the population in Zepa. I refer you to 65 ter 2941. These are notes of General Smith's meeting at 1420 in the afternoon of 13 July with Prime Minister Silajdzic. Parts of the notes state: "Both the prime minister and Minister Muratovic raised their concerns as to the as-yet unconfirmed reports of atrocities in the Srebrenica area." And further on, significantly: "They are also worried about reports of refugees being segregated into groups and men between the ages of 60 and 16 being sent to different locations." So, in addition to all the direct contribution to the men being transferred under his control, he's contributing to the coercive environment, to the terror in Zepa. There was also the argument made, how would Drago Nikolic, the same for Vinko Pandurevic's counsel made, how would they even know about directive 7, how would they even know about this forcible transfer? Mr. Thayer's gone through some of those documents, and I'll go through just a few. I'm not going to read out from all of them, but to just give you the ones which I think are significant, which show clearly that this criminal purpose, to remove the population from the enclaves as stated in many, many documents, reached all the way down to the battalion level and directly, in some cases, directly to the chief of security, Drago Nikolic. I'll start with directive 4, 65 ter 29 of 19 November 1992. I won't go through the text. But on page 5 of the English, it states that the Drina Corps' task is to force the Muslim population to leave the enclaves. 65 ter 3029 from the 24th of November, 1992, from the Drina Corps to the Zvornik Brigade, the first paragraph of the order: "Wear the enemy out, break it up, force them to surrender, and force the Muslim population to leave the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde." 65 ter 3177 from the Bratunac Brigade Command to the 3rd Infantry Battalion, going down to the battalion commander level. If you look at page 3, my friend read it out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I hate to interrupt my colleague, but maybe he can tell us where Drago Nikolic was in 1992. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could just continue, Your Honour. This is the information going to all of the brigades, all of the units, and down to the battalion level; and this one again states that the goal is to make life impossible so that the population leaves the enclave en masse, realising they can't survive there. 2667, 24th of July, 1994, a Drina Corps debriefing to the Zvornik Brigade, again to reduce the enclaves to Srebrenica town and Zepa. I won't go through directive 7, which has been discussed. 65 ter 838, which I believe is also 6D7, Krivaja-95, and we've already seen how the commander was fully aware of the goals of that operation and the Zvornik Brigade. 65 ter 817, a preparatory order for Krivaja-95, again distributed directly to the Zvornik Brigade on 2nd July 1995, paragraph 2 referencing that this order is carried out pursuant to directive 7. I think it's unlikely to cite to directives to the Command and assume that the brigade command has no idea what those directives being cited are. 65 ter 837, again related directly to Krivaja-95, directed to the Command, to the chief of security, to Drago Nikolic, referring to the preparatory orders which refer to directive 7. Paragraph 2.1D requires the formation of a protection squad of the commander and four soldiers from the military police company. So that's telling Drago Nikolic that the commander and four MPs need to be prepared for this operation. You could also look at 65 ter 110. This is the order from the Drina Corps to the Zvornik Brigade, requiring them to send buses and trucks for the forcible transfer to Bratunac. Of course, it's called an evacuation in the document. 65 ter 322, again the 12th of July, the response from the Zvornik Brigade. In paragraph 2: "We sent one Praga with crew to the area of the 8th Battalion in Kajici, which is near Kravica. We sent to Bratunac, pursuant to your order, eight buses from Drinatrans, two buses from our military post, and four of our trucks. One military police detachment was sent to Konjevic Polje pursuant to your order." Then 65 ter 330, the interim combat report from Vinko Pandurevic on the 16th of July, 1995. I won't read it out again, but he states that Krivaja-95 will not be complete as long as a single enemy civilian remains behind the front line. So, if you look at the evidence from Richard Butler, all the evidence, the role of the security chief of the brigade, for purposes of 98 bis certainly the argument that Drago Nikolic would have no idea about directive 7, no idea about the purpose of this operation, is simply not credible. The question of whether there was an attack on the civilian population, on a predominantly civilian population, that was raised by my friends. I don't think I really need to go into this, just to say that the evidence supports that there was an attack. The very same evidence before in Krstic and Blagojevic has been found to constitute legally, I'm speaking not about the evidence, but legally an attack upon the civilian population. I would refer you, though, to the testimony of Kingori on the 11 January 2008, at 19440 to 19442, where he describes how the reason the population fled, the reason they left, was not because they wanted to flee the enclave, leave the enclaves of their own free will. They were afraid of being killed. They are afraid of being bombarded. They were looking for any way out in order to survive. This testimony from Major Kingori is confirmed if you look at the testimony of Ahmo Hasic, PW-106, PW-110, PW-111, PW-112, PW-117, PW-120, and PW-127. It's also clear from the intercept, which has been referred to with General Mladic, 65 ter 1113, that everybody's going, those who want to go and those who don't. I won't go over -- I was going to go over the same topics for Zepa and that this was a coercive environment, but that's been covered by Mr. Thayer. I have less to say, and now I'll move on to Mr. Beara's submissions. Again, to begin with, I want to respond to submissions which I think have inadvertently, incorrectly, stated facts in the record. First, Mr. Ostojic stated that the record contains no evidence that Beara was anywhere in and around Srebrenica from 1 to 12 July 1995, except for the evidence of Celanovic, which he says is uncorroborated. Celanovic is one of three viva voce witnesses who saw Mr. Beara in the Srebrenica area in the time frame of 10-11-12 July. Celanovic stated he saw Beara and Popovic together in front of the Bratunac Brigade building on 10-11 July. That's at 6654 to 6655. Second, Bozo Momcilovic testified that he saw Beara and Popovic at the Pribicevac IKM in this time period 11 July, 14085-14088. PW-161 stated that he saw he saw Bratunac -- saw Beara in Bratunac one or two days before 13 July at the -- once in the Hotel Fontana and once passing by the Hotel Fontana. That's at 9362. The second assertion I want to address is that the only evidence that places Beara in Bratunac on the night of 13 July was the testimony of Celanovic and his evidence was unreliable, that this is the only evidence now about the 13th, not the days beforehand, and that the only questions Beara had with Celanovic was about questioning prisoners, which was entirely lawful. Remember, Mr. Beara, this is again relating to the forcible transfer, comes to Celanovic and tells him, "The prisoners are coming. They're coming to Bratunac, and you should check them. You should talk to them and look for IDs." There were other witnesses who saw Beara in Bratunac on that night. There is a -- there is the testimony from PW-161 again, that he met Beara in Deronjic's office in the SDS. He wasn't completely sure about the date; and that at about 1.00 or 2.00 a.m., on the morning of July 14th, PW-161 again met Beara at the SDS premises. That's at a time when there's a discussion about where to dig the graves for the people who were being killed. Mr. Beara states there were going to be a lot of bodies. There was again, in the duty officer notebook, 377 for 13 July, a reference: "The president of the municipality of Mitrovic called and asked that the flatbed trailer, Colonel Beara," which has been crossed out, "be sent to Bratunac and that they are passed along the message." It's also not correct to say that the only discussion was about questioning of the prisoners with Celanovic. If you look at 6639 to 6640, Celanovic explains that he said to

utterances.speaker: MR. BEARA
utterances.text: "And I said that I was worried because I went home or I needed to change because it was hot, and I saw there were too many people who were prisoners in town and too few soldiers, I mean Serb soldiers." And Beara replied: "All right. We'll have a look at that, and I'll hope they make it through the night. And we will, too, because I guess they're going to Kladanj tomorrow." And during the walk later that Mr. Celanovic has with Beara, where they see the Muslim prisoners on buses at the Vuk Karadzic School, on towards the stadium, this is at 6637, 6643, 6647, 6653, 6690 to 6700, there's a conversation during these places where they discuss not questioning of the prisoners but what's going to happen to the prisoners. Question: "What did he say about them?" Answer: "I asked him why these people weren't leaving immediately, why they were standing there; and he," Beara, "said that the transport had to be reorganised, that there were many people on the vehicles, that it wasn't safe to transport them that way, and that the vehicles had to be returned. The vehicles that took the women and children, that they would be reorganised and they would go to Kladanj the next morning." Question: "You said there were too many people on the vehicles for them to be transported that way?" Answer: "Actually, he said there were too few vehicles in order to transport them." In other words, Beara's response was: "Well, those vehicles are being used now to transfer out the women and children. We have to wait for them to come back, and then we'll start moving the prisoners." And, again, regarding his knowledge of what's going to happen to the prisoners, where they're going to be going, he told PW-161 that machinery would need to be prepared to go to Milici because there would be a lot of dead people who needed to be buried. PW-168 testified, 15843 -- actually, could we go into private for one moment just to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So, on the 13th of July, Mr. Beara's in Bratunac. He's by the schools where the prisoners are held. He's at the SDS office talking about the machinery that's going to be needed to bury the victims. He directs PW-161 to go to Glogova to dig pits that's for the Kravica victims, some of whom are probably still alive at that point in time. He's on intercept 11.30, 11.30 in the morning, talking about the prisoners at Konjevic Polje and what's going to happen to them, where they're going, calling them "balijas," saying, "Shove them on a playground. Who gives a fuck about them. Line them up in rows. Excellent if they're killing each other." The next point I want to address briefly is the carefully-phrased assertion that there was no evidence that Beara was near or around the area of Zepa at the commencement of the civilian population's transfer. There is, however, uncontested evidence that Beara was in Zepa during the operation. PW-109 saw Beara at the UN check-point near Zepa with Generals Mladic and General Krstic. This is at 14603 to 14604. Question: "Did you know a person by the name of Colonel Beara at that time?" Answer: "Yes." Question: "Did you see Colonel Beara anywhere around the Zepa area during the Zepa operation?" Answer: "I saw Colonel Beara at that check-point probably near the end of the Zepa operation. He was -- he was in that check-point. That's the only time I saw him there." "What was he doing?" "Well, he was in the company of General Mladic, General Krstic, and those security points of, you know, United Nations." The next page, 14605.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: "Your Honours, you'll be happy to know we have no questions." The next point, again on Zepa, Mr. Ostojic argued that his client's only involvement in Zepa could be seen by the three intercepts which were taken after the forcible transfer/deportation had ended. That's not accurate. Those intercepts are from the 1st and 2nd of August, and they are actually exculpatory because they show Beara acting in a very legal and professional manner. I won't go through those. I just ask Your Honours to take a look at those intercepts and see if you agree with Mr. Ostojic's assertion. Another of the Defences' argument is that Beara's only alleged involvement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to make things simpler, do you have the references for the three intercepts?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That would be 1380, 1381, 1395 is one I would also ask you to look at, and 1378.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very briefly, talking about the column, the men captured from the column or who surrendered, Mr. Ostojic said: "It deals not with civilians, it deals with Bosnian Muslim military and non-military men from the column. The Bosnian Muslims in the column who left, they left of their own volition and were not theoretically or practically forcibly removed." Well, first, I don't understand the distinction, saying that non-military from the men -- non-military men from the column and military men are not civilians, that non-military men are civilians. And, again, I'm not going to go through it again, but the coercion that forced the entire population to leave the enclave applied. These men were transferred, once they are captured, detained, and moved up to Bratunac from Sandici or wherever they had been brought and then to Zvornik. The last couple of points where I go to Mr. Ostojic's argument that Mr. Beara had nothing to do with men and the movement of men from the columns. If you look at 377 again, the duty officer logbook, 14 July at 1500, Colonel Beara is coming and order - there's a blank word - "Orahovac-Petkovci, Orahovac-Pilica." He's going to the places where many of these prisoners end up. Also, PW-104, at 7940 to 7942, he's at a meeting at Standard, at the Zvornik Brigade, with Mr. Beara, and Mr. Beara says, "We have a lot of prisoners, and it's very hard for us to control them. There are various locations in the Zvornik Municipality. We have to get rid of them." This is part of -- it's part of the chain. It's the movement, it's the end for many of them, the forcible transfer. Lastly, we heard the "empty vessel" argument and phrase again. If you look at 65 ter 1179, that's the intercept from the 15 July at 10.00 a.m.: "That vessel is completely filled." He is having difficulty carrying out the orders which he's been given, and he's under stress from it, if you read through this intercept. Beara begins: "General Furtula didn't carry out the boss' orders." Next he says: "I need 30 men, just like it was ordered." Further down: "I need 15 to 30 men with Boban Indjic. I can't do anything." He's talking about the orders he's received, and Krstic says at the end: "Now I will be the one to blame for these order not getting filled out, completed." The last point, Mr. Ostojic said there were no photographs of Beara with Mladic. Well, if you look at the video at 2025, we've got Beara, Mladic, Krstic, at the celebration for the Drina Wolves towards the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: (redacted) The meeting at Standard that Mr. Bircakovic testified about, where Beara and Popovic come to meet with Drago Nikolic, it's very early in the morning, beginning sometime he says around 7.00 or 8.00, he goes to fetch Drago and brings him to the meeting, and it's a short meeting of 15 to 20 minutes. That's at 11012 until 11015, 11097, and 11101 to 11102.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Lastly, Mr. Ostojic argued that adjudicated facts 203 and 219 show that the transfer of the population was complete by 2000 hours on 13 July 1995. That's not entirely accurate. Those facts relate just to what's going on with the civilian population in Potocari. Those facts don't state and there is no adjudicative fact that forcible transfer ended at that time. The indictment's clear that the forcible transfer ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The protected witness has been mentioned by mistake. I'm going to deal with it.

utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. Mr. Nicholls, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I do realise I did mention that name. Thank you for catching it. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Kwon did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Again, the indictment is clear when the forcible transfer, we say, ended. It was not 13 July, in the evening. That concludes my responses to my friends' representations last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We're just about at the break, I think.

utterances.text: Yes. But I want to know whether you are -- are you coming back, Mr. Thayer, on other things?

utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm prepared to submit with respect to Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll deal with that a little later. We'll have a 25-minute break now. The time is, according to the transcript, 12.19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think we'll certainly be able to finish the submission with respect to Mr. Borovcanin today. As I mentioned, Mr. McCloskey originally was going to provide the Prosecution's submission, but I'm standing in today. So I'll get right to it. The evidence we heard begins on the Trnovo battlefield on or about the 10th of July, when the RS Ministry of the Interior issues its order to Mr. Borovcanin to assemble a task force, a combined combat group. He then reports to Bratunac, and we're underway. The evidence before the Chamber establishes that Mr. Borovcanin was in command of forces which entered Potocari on the morning of 12 July 1995. Among those forces were members of the Special Police Brigade, 2nd Sekovici Detachment, as well as members of the Jahorina training facility whom I will refer to as deserters for ease of reference. You heard testimony from, among others, PW-160; from Mendeljejev Djuric, known as Mane Djuric; from various PJP members; from Special Police Brigade members, and I'll talk about the testimony of Messrs. Celic and Pepic; and, of course, we heard the testimony of PW-100. This is in addition to various Dutch-Bat officers who encountered members of Mr. Borovcanin's forces in Potocari on the 12th and 13th of July. On the 12th, there is evidence before this Trial Chamber that various members of this combined unit deployed throughout Potocari in part to surround the compound, to clear the surrounding areas and homes, and, as we'll hear, ultimately to assist in the separation of the Muslim men from their families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I hate to interfere in my colleague's submission, but it has really nothing to do with the submission that I made pursuant to 98 bis. I had only two topics. These were paragraph 8 and paragraph 2 of the indictment. All this has nothing to do with the submission that I made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What's your comment on that? Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think, I hope we've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're supposed to be replying. You're moving nothing, as such. The ball is in actually the court of the Defence for the Rule 98 bis purposes. Your task is to just respond to what the Defence submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: As I understand it, then, that will pretty much be limited to the conspiracy count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's count 2 and count 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Count 2 and count 8. Now, to the extent that, I think, we've tried to make our position clear, that the road to Zepa, as it were, has a beginning in Potocari, then I'll just limit my comments to what we've already stated, that with respect to the men who were deported in Zepa, who made that fateful choice to cross the river, that was -- those coercive conditions were created through the actions of Mr. Borovcanin's forces in Potocari along the road from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac. The VRS doesn't get to go to Zepa until the men are separated out in Potocari, until the men who are trying to break through are captured, and that element is removed. It is, again, Mr. Borovcanin's men who are assisting in separating these men in Potocari who are marked for death. It is his men who are arresting, capturing, robbing, detaining, and transporting the unarmed prisoners in the area of Sandici to the Kravica warehouse; and they, too, are marked for death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise again, and I really have to say if my colleague is suggesting something, then he could, he should go straight to our arguments. I mean, again this is not something that we argued in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Thayer, why don't you go straight and answer or reply to the submissions of Mr. Lazarevic, such as his relationship with Petrusic or the journalist and his non-involvement in relation to the last count?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, where I believe the relevance lies in the evidence I've just described is that this is, at the very least, the type of circumstantial evidence from which a reasonable tribunal of fact could infer the intent necessary under the conspiracy to commit genocide count. Now, with respect to, for example, Mr. Petrovic, I don't know if the Chamber has had an opportunity to read the article or, for that matter, really familiarise itself with the transcript of the recording, but Mr. Petrovic testified that he and Mr. Borovcanin had mutual respect for each other. The question was raised: Well, why would anybody who is part of a JCE permit that to happen? Well, first, when we actually look at the tapes, as they were edited by Mr. Petrovic, and you'll recall Mr. Nicholls' careful presentation of that evidence, there was an attempt to -- for the tapes that were made public, to take that portion of the Kravica warehouse execution clip out of sequence. It's our submission that that's evidence of a consciousness of what that really meant and what that was really portraying, that there were these efforts by Mr. Petrovic to move things around. You'll recall there's certain black spots or gaps on one of the versions. And when you are spending this type of time with somebody with whom you have a relationship of mutual respect, well, I think it's not controversial that you're going to trust that other person not to hurt you, not to do anything that's going to damage your interests. My friend stated that there's no evidence that Srebrenica and Zepa was a unified objective, and I hope we've made it clear that this was a unitary objective from the beginning, that Srebrenica and Zepa were linked from the inception of this common purpose to move out the Muslim population from these enclaves. They were perceived as one, one threat, one obstacle, to a border between the Serb states that they wished to establish. Mr. Borovcanin's participation in the cleansing of Potocari, the forcible removal of that population, is part and parcel, as Mr. Nicholls argued, of what happened in Zepa. And, again, that contributes to the reasonable fear on the part of the men who had to make that choice to cross the Drina River. And I don't think I have anything else to add, given the narrowness of my friend's submission. I can try to answer questions for the Court, but I think the conspiracy case law is pretty clear and I think we have adduced sufficient evidence under at least the standard for 98 bis to support Mr. Borovcanin's participation in that conspiracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm very grateful to my colleague for putting this clear now, but there is one thing that I believe needs to be clarified, and this is not my reply. I would just like to say that it seems that there is a misinterpretation of evidence from the transcript of the testimony of Mr. Petrovic. It does not appear that he was the one who edited the tape, but quite the opposite. Once the tape was brought to Belgrade, there were other men who were in possession of it, of the tape, and who edited it and then broadcasted it. Just that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon and, for that matter, all other Defence teams, we have discussed briefly during the break whether we are to grant even the shortest of replies, and our position remains as it was in the beginning. We don't wish to grant right of reply to any one of you. We think we can fully distinguish the wheat from the chaff and move ahead, and restrict ourselves to what is strictly necessary for the purpose of Rule 98 bis. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The position is that we will now rise and withdraw, and we'll start our deliberations. Since we finished these submissions earlier than expected, it's very likely that the decision that we will be handing down will come earlier. As of now, I don't think we are in a definitive position to say exactly on which date it will be, but we'll work as much as we can, go through all the submissions that we consider relevant, and I'm sure that halfway through our deliberations, we should be in a position to inform you of the exact date when we will hand down the decision, which will be oral; but, of course, we will have to have bullet points and other things available before we can proceed with the oral decision. Okay. I thank you very much also for your practical approach to the matter, which shows that you have a pretty full understanding of what really Rule 98 bis is all about; and at the same level, we hope to be able to come back to you with a reasoned decision shortly. Thank you.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.10 p.m.,
